implementation_notes: In Rust the reply channel is usually an owned handle inside the request value rather than a header: the requester creates a oneshot::channel(), moves the Sender into the request struct and awaits the Receiver, so the reply path is compile-time checked and needs no addressing. This is the shape of actor-style services (mailbox plus per-request oneshot) and of tower-style service calls; the broker header appears only when requests leave the process — see the lapin variant.

variants.name: oneshot::Sender carried in the request struct
variants.implementation_notes: In Rust the reply channel is usually an owned handle inside the request value rather than a header: the requester creates a oneshot::channel(), moves the Sender into the request struct and awaits the Receiver, so the reply path is compile-time checked and needs no addressing. This is the shape of actor-style services (mailbox plus per-request oneshot) and of tower-style service calls; the broker header appears only when requests leave the process — see the lapin variant.
pitfalls: Sender::send returns Err when the Receiver was dropped: ignoring it turns 'requester left' into a silently lost reply, so map it to a cancellation path.
A oneshot is single-consume and not cloneable — fan-out or duplicate replies need an mpsc or broadcast channel instead.
Keeping the Sender alive in a longer-lived struct keeps the requester's future pending; dropping the request is the cancellation signal.

variants.name: AMQP BasicProperties reply_to (lapin)
variants.implementation_notes: Over AMQP, lapin exposes the address on the message: BasicProperties is a builder whose with_reply_to sets the property, and the consumer reads delivery.properties.reply_to() and publishes the answer there, exactly as other AMQP clients do. Choose it when replies must cross process boundaries, survive a restart, or be inspectable by the broker; keep the oneshot variant for same-process services where a queue name would be pure overhead.
pitfalls: The delivery must be acked or nacked; publishing the reply before acking a request that later fails produces duplicate replies.
reply_to is Option<String>: a request without it needs an explicit policy (fixed channel or dead-letter), never an unwrap.
lapin's properties are builder values, not mutable — build a fresh BasicProperties for the reply instead of reusing the request's.
Sender::send returns Err when the Receiver was dropped: ignoring it turns 'requester left' into a silently lost reply, so map it to a cancellation path.
A oneshot is single-consume and not cloneable — fan-out or duplicate replies need an mpsc or broadcast channel instead.
Keeping the Sender alive in a longer-lived struct keeps the requester's future pending; dropping the request is the cancellation signal.
